Introduction
A picture is worth a thousand words. Literally! Figures may be one of the most important parts of communicating science in a journal article, yet the least discussed in scientific writing. Not only does a figure visually communicate your findings in ways that  words can’t describe , but they literally do take up space that could otherwise be filled with a thousand words in the manuscript.  As such, figures  and their captions are critical piece of scientific  literature,  and they must strike a careful balance between capitalizing on visual communication while sacrificing space that would otherwise be filled with text. Strategically placed figures can also give the reader a time to rest after paragraphs of reading  while poorly  placed  figures  interrupt the flow of communication.  Your job as a scientific writer is to artfully craft a story striking the perfect balance in providing just enough information for the reader to understand your story without taking them on side quests that pull them away from the leading narrative of your study. But don’t be fooled. This is no easy task and takes careful thought and consideration of every detail included in figures and their captions. So how do you achieve the perfect figures? Keep reading belo w ! 

Part  1  –  P ainting  a picture  (or table) 
To state the obvious, this whole thing starts with the perfect figure.  A good figure highlights patterns in data from your study.  Figures can communicate relationships between variables that numbers cannot and help the reader draw quick comparisons between different datasets. Since figures are most often communicating complex scientific information, often unique to an individual study, it is crucial that figures  are easy to understand.  Figures should be able to be interpreted as standalone data without text and that includes the figure caption.  As simple as this seems, most scientists struggle to achieve  this,  and many bad figures end up in publications . 

Top tips for a good figure
- **Simple figures are best.**  You don’t want to  burden  the reader with an overcomplicated figure that requires deep thought to interpret. Ask yourself “is there any way to simplify this figure without losing key information?”  
- **Maintain a visual hierarchy.**  The most important information should stick out to the reader first. As an example, if you are showing a figure of number of plane crashes and the size of the planes that crashed you want the number of plane crashes to stand out before the size of the planes.  
- **Use common types of figures** **.**  It is much easier for a reader to interpret a figure type they have seen before. There are infinite ways to visually communicate your data and choosing the right one is essential. Using abstract figure types will cause the reader to spend more energy learning how to interpret your results. Using a box plot for example may seem boring but the goal is not to be unique, it is to communicate your results. Your results should be the most interesting part of the figure anyways, not how the figure looks. 
- **L** **egib** **ility**  **at different scales.**  This applies both to the size  of the figure elements and of the text included in the figure. Publications may reduce or enlarge the size of the figures you submit. The size of the figure may also change for the reader depending on the pla t form they are viewing your figure on so aiming for figure text and elements to be on the larger size is always best.  
- **Proper use of numbers.**  Numbers can be challenging for readers to interpret and should be used intentionally and sparingly.  Use numbers in figures when there are lots of numbers and the reader would benefit from visual representation of them and their relationship. For instances with a few numbers these can be referenced directly in the results and discussion sections.  

Many of these tips may seem obvious however they are commonly forgotten. Most readers have had at least one experience when reading a paper where their eyebrow furls trying to decode an overcomplicated figure. An equally important way to review your figures before submission to a publication is to go over the common pitfalls of a bad figure. 

The common pitfalls of a bad figure
- **Overcomplicat** **ed figures** **.**  Including too much information in too little space will overwhelm the reader and make it challenging to identify the key messages and narrative in the figure. 
- **Too many numbers** **.**  Numbers can be laboursome for a reader to interpret as they must be related to the context of the  variable  they are representing in order to be interpreted. Equally, including redundant numbers to inflate your results can also be burdensome to the  r eader.  As an example, saying “ L andslides covered 0.9% of the island (45 hectares) in 2023 and grew to 0.95% of the island (47.5 hectares) in 2024 . ” both inflates the numbers and is redundant as the hectares and percentages represent the same thing. This makes more work for the reader to compare  both values . 
- **Misleading figure scales** **.**  Make sure that the scales of your X-axis and Y-axis match in a way that is not misleading and matches the relationship that the variables have to each other.  If comparing two  panels  make sure that the scales in the x and y axis are the same across panels. 
- **Including trend lines or fit lines when there isn’t a statistically significant**  **relationship.**  Don’t  falsely  advertise  your results . C onsider what  showing data without a statistically significant relationship means to your reader . Should you include this at all or is the key result th e fact  there isn’t a relationship? 
- **Improper use of colour** **.**  Many colours have an associated meaning ( e.g.  blue for water, green for plans, red for hot, etc). Ensure that the colours chosen for your figures are appropriate to the data they represent. Also ensure that you are using colour pallets that  can still be interpreted by people with colour  impairment .  

More detailed design advice for figures
- You don’t need a figure title – that can go in the caption.
- Include enough white space for legibility.
- Use colour when appropriate and choose colour palettes that are colour-blind friendly. A large portion of the population has some level of colour  impairment,  and you want to ensure that your results are interpretable by everyone. 
- Use acronyms appropriately. Yes, they are a great way to cut down on text to save space, but it can get confusing to the reader to remember many new acronyms.  No one likes acronym soup.
- Don’t forget about colour-word associations.  E.g.  If I make a map of ALDs that are blue, the reader would probably think that the landslides are water rather than landslides . 
- Keep a consistent style across figures to make for a clean look  and to improve legibility. This includes colour palettes, font, font sizes, visual elements, etc. 
- Don’t include too many panels  or l egends . 

Using tables instead of figures
Tables are great at communicating data with many variables or observations that are not easily synthesized. Tables can also be useful to synthesize data which may not have a clear pattern, for example a table with the number of the drone flights flown at each study site and when they were flown. Or the ice content, carbon content, depth, etc. of 12 permafrost cores that were sampled. It is also an efficient way for the reader to pull information to use in other studies. They are also used when reporting of precise numbers is necessary.  Tables however are bad at showing patterns in a dataset. Do not use a table when the reader must interpret a relationship between a large range of numbers.  

Some best practices in table design are:
- Represent patterns horizontally, not  vertically 
- Simplify tables to minimum numbers of columns and  rows 
- Think critically about significant digits, how many decimal places are  required 
- Order columns in order of importance but also in an intuitive way for the reader. For  example  many tables are ordered thematically by study site

P art  2 :  Describing the  picture 
This part may seem simple but there is an art to it.  Writing figure captions isn’t about describing the figure , i t’s about describing the meaning behind the figure . It’s  about  the art of  including just the right amount of information to the reader to disseminate the  figures  message without leading to confusion . Luckily for you there is a simple formula to achieve the perfect figure caption. 

Formula for a good figure caption
1. Main point to take away from figure (1-2 sentences)
- Could include two main takeaway messages if they are equally important.
2. Further explanation of figure. (3 or more sentences)
- Explain abbreviations, symbols, interpretation of colours used, etc.

That’s it!  Simple as pie.  Other recommendations and pitfalls are outlined below . 

**Tips for the perfect figure caption**
- Lead with meaning , follow with detail and explanation . 
- Multiple numbers to describe the same statistic should not be used . 
- Figure captions can be as long as needed. Some figure captions are as big as paragraphs.
- Both the figure and the figure caption should be able to stand alone as separate pieces of information. Make sure that you have described everything in the figure that is essential for the reader to be able to make sense of the important results without needing to visually analyze the figure.

**Common pitfalls for figure captions**
- Describing the data rather than the interpretation of the data . 
- Describing what the figure looks like, rather than what it means . 
- Not defining abbreviations
- Not explaining symbols, colours, etc.
- Improper order of key results.
- Not enough information to stand alone as a source of information. 

Figure caption example – The Last Supper
The easiest way to solidify your understanding of what good and bad figure captions looks like is of course through examples.  Let’s go through an example of a bad figure caption versus a good figure caption using the last supper, a famous painting by Leonardo Di Caprio.  

Below  is what a bad figure caption loo k s  like: 

![](data:image/png;base64,)
Figure X.  Twelve  men sit at a table eating bread  and drinking wine . Bread represents the body and wine represents blood. This is a scene from the bible painted in 1800  by  Leonardo Da Vinci .  The twelve  apostles  gather to  discuss that there  has been a  betrayel . 

What went bad ?  The painting d escribes the scene and what the symbols represent but doesn’t describe the takeaway or the meaning of the scene. You are left wondering what the purpose of the painting was - but why are they all  gathered  to eat the body and blood of Christ?  Who are the people in this painting and why are they so important?  Following the principles of the perfect figure caption, th e leading takeaway from this paintin g  is that there are twelve men drinking bread and drinking wine. The writer then moves onto discussing the symbolism behind the bread and wine which is appropriate except that they do so before their final  sentence which outlines the true meaning of the painting. 

Here’s what a good figure caption  sh ould look like: 

![](data:image/png;base64,)Figure X. The Last Supper is the final meal Jesus shared with his apostles in Jerusalem  before his crucifixion, where he instituted the Eucharist (Communion). During this Passover meal, Jesus identified bread as his body and wine as his blood of the new covenant, washed his disciples' feet to teach humility, and predicted his betrayal by Judas Iscariot.  This scene was painted in 1800 by Leonardo Da Vinci, depicting this biblical scene from the gospel of John.  

This  figure caption leads with meaning of the painting, followed by further detail on the symbolism behind the bread and wine, why people are gathered and discussing amongst each other anxiously, and provides detail on the artist who painted the scene.

Part  3  –  Artful  figure selection 
Now that we’ve talked about how to make the best figures and figure captions let’s discuss how to choose which figures you should include in your manuscript. First and foremost, you need to decide which journal you plan to submit your paper to (if you haven’t already) and look up the journal requirements. Different journals have different  allotments  for how many figures you can include as well as formatting requirements for those figures. If you are submitting to a research letter for example, that is a shorter form  journal  and you may only be able to submit 3-5 figures. Most often we have way more figures than that which is when figure selection becomes key. This is when you want to lay out  all of  your figures and choose which  four  distil  the story of your research most simply and provide the most meaningful context for concepts or results that are challenging to explain. For example, it may be more important to your research that you have a figure on how landslides have increased in area over time rather than a map of your study sites. Although both are important, one better describes. Readers may only read the abstract and figures. A good exercise is to pick which figures best tell the story of a paper.

Summary of chapter
In this chapter we discussed figure design, when and how to use a table, how to write effective figure/table captions and  strategic placement of figures and tables. We also went over various examples and exercises to hammer this content home. 

To summarize the main points discussed in the chapter:

- To have the perfect figure is best visually communicate your results, literally spell them out in the caption and artfully place them within the manuscript where it adds to the narrative without interrupting it. 
- Figures and their captions should be a  standalone  piece of the manuscript. That means that the reader should be able to read the figure and the figure caption without reading the rest of the manuscript and have a good understanding of the message the figures aim to convey . 

Now you are practiced and ready to embark on your own journey of visually communicating your research to the world!
